chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from al-Nadhr ibn Suwayd, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam, that he asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about the Names of Allah and their derivation: From what is 'Allah' derived?

He said: So he said to me: O Hisham, 'Allah' is derived from 'ilah' (god/deity), and 'al-ilah' connotes the one who is worshipped. The name is other than the named. Whoever worships the name without the meaning has disbelieved and has not worshipped anything. Whoever worships the name and the meaning has disbelieved and worshipped two. Whoever worships the meaning without the name, that is true monotheism. Have you understood, O Hisham?

He said: I said: Increase for me. He said: Indeed, Allah has ninety-nine names. If the name were identical to the named, then every one of these names would be a god. But Allah is a meaning to which these names point, and each of them is other than Him. O Hisham, 'bread' is a name for what is eaten, 'water' is a name for what is drunk, 'clothes' is a name for what is worn, 'fire' is a name for what burns. Have you understood, O Hisham, with an understanding by which you can repel and contend with our enemies and those who take other than Allah as a deity?
I said: Yes. He said: May Allah benefit you by it and make you firm, O Hisham. Hisham said: By Allah, no one has defeated me in the subject of Monotheism until I stood in this position.
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the name of God and His essence in Shia theology?
ai.summary: This hadith, narrated by the rationalist scholar Hisham ibn al-Hakam, elucidates the Shia theological distinction between the divine name (ism) and the divine essence (dhat), asserting that 'Allah' is a linguistic signifier rather than the essence itself. The Imam uses the analogy of bread and water to demonstrate that while all ninety-nine names point to the One Essence, they are not identical to it, thereby refuting the notion that each name constitutes a separate deity. This nuanced understanding of Tawhid safeguards against both anthropomorphism and polytheism, establishing a foundation for Shia creedal precision.

en.ammaar-muslim: 10. [10/307] al-Kafi: Ali b. Ibrahim from his father from al-Nadhr b. Suwayd from Hisham b. al-Hakam - that he asked Aba Abdillah عليه السلام about the Names of Allah and their derivation saying: What is Allah derived from?

He (Hisham) said: so he (the Imam) said to me: O Hisham, ‘Allah’ is derived from ‘ilah’ and ‘al-ilah’ connotes the one who is worshipped. The name is other than the named. Whoever worships the name without the meaning then he has disbelieved and has not worshipped anything. Whoever worships the name and the meaning then he has disbelieved and worshipped two (distinct things). Whoever worships the meaning without the name then that is true monotheism. Have you understood O Hisham?

He (Hisham) said: I said: increase for me. He said: Allah has ninety nine names, if the name was identical to what is named then every name among these (ninety-nine) would be a god, rather Allah is a meaning to which these names point to, and each one of them is other than him. O Hisham, ‘bread’ is a name for what is eaten, ‘water’ is a name for what is drunk, ‘clothes’ is a name for what is worn, ‘fire’ is a name for what burns, have you understood Hisham? an understanding through which you can repel and defeat our enemies and those who betake others apart from Allah Mighty and Majestic.
I said: Yes. He said: May Allah benefit you by it and make you firm O Hisham. Hisham said: by Allah no one has defeated me on the subject of Tawhid to this day when I stand in the position I do.
